procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated in the provided text, but implied to be a lower court in Andhra Pradesh since the High Court heard an appeal.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated July 3, 1968, of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 883 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Andhra Pradesh High Court allowed the appeal, convicted the appellant under s. 92 for contravention of s. 6 ( 1) and rules 3 and 5 ( 3), and sentenced him to pay a fine of Rs. 50 under each count.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court after obtaining special leave to appeal the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the appeal.

facts: More than 20 persons regularly worked on the premises, performing tasks such as stripping stalks from tobacco leaves.
The appellant (the company) contended that these individuals were not 'workers' but were employed by independent contractors.
The prosecution provided positive evidence from a witness (P.W.1) that the work was performed under the supervision of the management.
The appellant suggested the workers were employed by independent contractors during cross-examination but did not produce any evidence to support this claim or to rebut the prosecution's evidence.
law: The definition of a 'worker' is provided in Section 2(1) of the Factories Act.
A 'worker' is a person employed, directly or through an agency, in any manufacturing process.
The court interpreted this definition to require a relationship of master and servant between the management and the person employed.
The onus of proving that the individuals were employed by the management, and were therefore 'workers', was on the prosecution.
application: The court determined that the prosecution had successfully discharged its burden of proof.
The prosecution adduced prima facie evidence showing that a master-servant relationship existed, primarily through witness testimony that the work was done under the 'supervision of the management'.
The court found the appellant's claim that the individuals were employed by independent contractors to be an unsubstantiated 'suggestion' that was 'not borne out by the materials on the record'.
Because the appellant failed to produce any rebutting evidence to counter the prosecution's evidence of supervision, the court accepted the prosecution's position.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the persons employed were 'workers' as defined in Section 2(1) of the Factories Act because the prosecution proved they worked under the supervision of the management, establishing a master-servant relationship, and the appellant failed to provide any evidence to the contrary.

issue.issue_text: whether any manufacturing process was being carried on therein

facts: At the company's premises in Eluru, sun-cured tobacco leaves were subjected to several processes.
These processes included moistening the leaves by sprinkling water on them to make them handleable without breakage.
The stalks were stripped from the leaves.
The leaves were then bundled and packed into gunny bags to be transported to the company's main factory in Bombay.
law: The Court referred to the definition of "manufacturing process" in Section 2(k)(i) of the Factories Act.

This section defines a manufacturing process as any process for "making, altering, repairing, ornamenting, finishing, packing, oiling, washing, cleaning, breaking up, demolishing or otherwise treating or adapting any article or substance with a view to its use, sale, transport, delivery or disposal."
The Court noted that this definition is "widely worded."
application: The Court applied the legal definition to the specific activities taking place at the premises.
It determined that moistening the tobacco leaves was a form of "adaptation" of the article.
It found that stripping the stalks from the leaves constituted "breaking them up."
The act of bundling the leaves and putting them into gunny bags was identified as "packing."
The Court observed that all these processes were done "with a view to their use and transport," which aligns with the purpose specified in the statutory definition.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the activities of moistening (adaptation), stripping (breaking up), and packing the tobacco leaves all fell within the wide definition of a "manufacturing process" under Section 2(k)(i) of the Factories Act.

appellant_arguments: The persons employed on the premises were not 'workers' but were employed by independent contractors.
respondent_arguments: The persons were 'workers' because the work of stripping stalks from tobacco leaves was done under the supervision of the management, establishing a master-servant relationship.
The prosecution adduced prima facie evidence of this relationship through the testimony of the Assistant Inspector of Factories (PW1).

arguments.issue_text: whether any manufacturing process was being carried on therein
appellant_arguments: The appellant initially produced an order from the Chief Inspector of Factories and a letter from the Superintendent of Central Excise to suggest the premises were not a factory, but later conceded that these documents were not relevant to the question.
respondent_arguments: A manufacturing process, specifically the work of stripping stalks from tobacco leaves, was being carried on in the premises, as evidenced by the testimony of the Assistant Inspector of Factories (PW1) and his inspection report.

cases.case_name: Sri Chintaman Rao & anr. v. State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.principle: For giving a restricted meaning to the words "directly or through an agency" in s. 2(l) and holding that a worker was a person employed by the management and that there must be a contract of service and a relationship of master and servant.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The onus of proving that workmen are employed by management rests on the prosecution; this onus is discharged if the prosecution adduces prima facie evidence of a master-servant relationship and the management fails to produce any rebutting evidence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court held that the company's premises at Eluru were a factory within the meaning of the Factories Act, 1948. This conclusion was based on the finding that the prosecution had successfully discharged its burden of proof in establishing that the persons employed therein were 'workers' under the management's employ, and not independent contractors as the appellant had suggested without supporting evidence.
legal_tests_applied: The onus of proving that the workmen were employed by the management was on the prosecution.
Application of the definition of 'workers' as defined in s. 2 (1) of the Factories Act, 1948.
Application of the definition of 'factory' within the meaning of s. 2(m) of the Factories Act, 1948.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's suggestion that the workmen were employed by independent contractors was rejected by the court as it was 'not borne out by the materials on the record.'

The documents produced by the appellant to argue the premises were not a factory were deemed irrelevant, a point the appellant's own counsel conceded and the court agreed with, stating the documents 'throw no. light on the qljtStion whether in 1966 the pr~ mises were a factory.'
why_respondent_won: The prosecution successfully discharged its onus of proving that the workmen were employed by the management.
Based on the evidence, the court made a direct holding that 'the persons employed are workers as defined in s. 2 (1).'
